In [[mathematics]], in the realm of [[group theory]], a [[Group (mathematics)|group]] is said to be a '''CA-group''' or '''centralizer abelian group''' if the [[centralizer]] of any non-[[identity element|identity]] element is an [[abelian group|abelian]] [[subgroup]].  [[Finite group|Finite]] CA-groups are of historical importance as an early example of the type of classifications that would be used in the [[Feit–Thompson theorem]] and the [[classification of finite simple groups]].  Several important infinite groups are CA-groups, such as [[free group]]s, [[Tarski monster]]s, and some [[Burnside group]]s, and the [[locally finite group|locally finite]] CA-groups have been classified explicitly.  CA-groups are also called '''commutative-transitive groups''' (or '''CT-groups''' for short) because commutativity is a [[transitive relation]] amongst the non-identity elements of a group if and only if the group is a CA-group.

==History==
Locally finite CA-groups were classified by several mathematicians from 1925 to 1998.  First, finite CA-groups were shown to be [[simple group|simple]] or [[solvable group|solvable]] in {{harv|Weisner|1925}}.  Then in the [[Brauer–Suzuki–Wall theorem]] {{harv|Brauer|Suzuki|Wall|1958}}, finite CA-groups of even [[order (group theory)|order]] were shown to be [[Frobenius group]]s, abelian groups, or {{nowrap|2-dimensional}} [[projective special linear group]]s over a [[finite field]] of even order, PSL(2, 2<sup>''f''</sup>) for ''f'' ≥ 2. Finally, finite CA-groups of odd order were shown to be Frobenius groups or abelian groups in {{harv|Suzuki|1957}}, and so in particular, are never nonabelian simple.

CA-groups were important in the context of the [[classification of finite simple groups]]. [[Michio Suzuki (mathematician)|Michio Suzuki]] showed that every finite, simple, nonabelian CA-group is of even order. This result was first extended to the Feit–Hall–Thompson theorem showing that finite, simple, nonabelian [[CN-group]]s had even order, and then to the [[Feit–Thompson theorem]] which states that every finite, simple, nonabelian group is of even order.  A textbook exposition of the classification of finite CA-groups is given as example 1 and 2 in {{harv|Suzuki|1986|pp=291–305}}.  A more detailed description of the Frobenius groups appearing is included in {{harv|Wu|1998}}, where it is shown that a finite, solvable CA-group is a [[semidirect product]] of an abelian group and a fixed-point-free automorphism, and that conversely every such semidirect product is a finite, solvable CA-group.  Wu also extended the classification of Suzuki et al. to [[locally finite group]]s.

==Examples==
Every abelian group is a CA-group, and a group with a non-[[trivial group|trivial]] [[center (group theory)|center]] is a CA-group if and only if it is abelian.  The finite CA-groups are classified: the solvable ones are semidirect products of abelian groups by [[cyclic group]]s such that every non-trivial element acts fixed-point-freely and include groups such as the [[dihedral group]]s of order 4''k''+2, and the [[alternating group]] on 4 points of order 12, while the nonsolvable ones are all simple and are the {{nowrap|2-dimensional}} projective special linear groups PSL(2, 2<sup>''n''</sup>) for ''n'' ≥ 2. Infinite CA-groups include free groups, [[PSL2(R)|PSL(2, '''R''')]], and [[Burnside group]]s of large [[prime number|prime]] exponent, {{harv|Lyndon|Schupp|2001|p=10}}.  Some more recent results in the infinite case are included in {{harv|Wu|1998}}, including a classification of locally finite CA-groups.  Wu also observes that [[Tarski monster]]s are obvious examples of infinite simple CA-groups.
